configuration.note: A line layer is read from a file, taken from the border two study areas share, or drawn on a map. A drawn line needs two positions at least; one click is a place, not a route, and the refusal says so and stays on screen. At most 200 lines are drawn one by one, past which a file is the right instrument. A drawn layer carries source 'drawn' so a reader can tell an observation somebody made from a file somebody published.

ports.note: The two areas are inputs only where the layer is a border, and then both are required: the border is the stretch of the first's outline within the stated distance of the second's. Read from a file, the layer has no inputs.

ontology.note: No ontology mapping yet, and no receipt of its own: the lines are handed on as GeoJSON, and a border's source names the two areas and the distance.

changes.description: Routes and flows drawn on a map, as pushpins place points: click to lay down each position, finish the line, name it. The order of clicking IS the direction, so a flow drawn from a camp to a clinic is not the same as one drawn the other way, and the editor shows both ends and offers to reverse. A drawn layer keeps its lines and names no file, because there is none. A layer set to be drawn with nothing drawn is refused in those words rather than being told to read a GPX.

evidence.note: Unit tested: the order of clicking as the direction, reversing without redrawing, a repeated click as one position, a one-position line refused with how to continue it, names that never collide, the 200-line limit, and a drawn layer reopening to be added to. Browser tested on Chromium: a route drawn on the map, refused at one position, finished, named, reversed, applied and run, reaching the Map it is wired to. NOT established: that anything checks a drawn route against the ground it was drawn over.
